common_name: Clyde Redmond Louisiana Iris (Classic Deep Blue Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Clyde Redmond is a widely grown, classic Louisiana iris cultivar producing large, richly colored deep blue-violet flowers in mid-spring, a color long considered one of the standards against which other blue Louisiana iris cultivars are judged. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape where many other perennials would struggle. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: President Hedley Louisiana Iris (Historic Reddish-Purple Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. President Hedley is a historically significant Louisiana iris cultivar from the early era of Louisiana iris breeding, producing rich reddish-purple flowers that helped establish the modern range of colors available in cultivated Louisiana iris hybrids. Like other Louisiana iris selections it performs best in reliably moist to wet soil and is an excellent choice for pond margins, ditch banks, and rain gardens where standing water is common after rain. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Ellen Bosanquet Crinum (Classic Wine-Red Fragrant Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Ellen Bosanquet is one of the most celebrated crinum cultivars for its rich, deep wine-red, fragrant flowers.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Ellen Bosanquet is widely regarded as one of the finest crinum lily cultivars ever introduced, producing large clusters of intensely fragrant, deep wine-red, trumpet-shaped flowers held on tall, sturdy scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage. Once established, the massive bulb persists and multiplies for decades with essentially no care, making it a classic pass-along plant of old Southern gardens and cemeteries. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil conditions with ease, and division is rarely necessary, since crinum bulbs actually bloom best when left undisturbed and slightly crowded.

common_name: Cecil Houdyshel Crinum (Classic Soft Pink Fragrant Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Cecil Houdyshel is one of the most reliably free-flowering crinum cultivars, often reblooming several times through the growing season.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Cecil Houdyshel produces abundant clusters of soft pink, sweetly fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers on tall scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage, and is known among crinum enthusiasts for blooming repeatedly through the warm season rather than in just a single flush, giving more overall color than many other crinum cultivars. Like other crinums it is extremely long-lived and low-maintenance once established, tolerating heat, humidity, and a range of soils, and it rarely if ever needs division since the bulbs bloom best when left undisturbed for many years.

common_name: Sulphur Queen Spider Lily (Yellow-Flowered Hymenocallis Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sulphur Queen is a yellow-flowered spider lily cultivar, a less common color than the more typical white-flowered hymenocallis types.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sulphur Queen produces the same delicate, spidery, fragrant flowers typical of hymenocallis, but in an unusual soft yellow rather than the classic white of most spider lily cultivars, giving a fresh color option for the summer bulb border. The strappy, dark green foliage stays attractive through the growing season, and the fragrant blooms open over several weeks in summer, drawing evening pollinators like moths. It multiplies slowly by offset bulbs to form an expanding clump over time and is generally low-maintenance once established, needing only routine watering during dry spells and winter mulch protection in the cooler parts of its range.
